gaps: Gives no cell-constant-to-range mapping. Sections 2.1 and 3.3 both tell the user to pick a probe by cell constant and both point at figure 6.3-1 as the guidance; only the figure's caption survives in the corpus, so no cell-constant value (per centimeter) is ever paired with a specific conductance range and 'which cell constant should I use for water around 500 microsiemens per centimeter' is unanswerable from this document.

States no recalibration interval in time. The only cadences given are 'check or calibrate before every field trip' and the annual NFQA proficiency sample; the document says frequent recalibration is generally unnecessary but never says how long a calibration remains valid, nor gives a daily, weekly, or per-deployment recalibration requirement.

Section 1.0 says specific conductance is often measured continually at USGS streamgages, but the document gives no procedure for a continuously deployed sonde: no allowable drift per day of deployment, no fouling-check or cleaning interval for a deployed conductivity cell, and no data-qualification rule for a drifting record. Every procedure in the chapter is for an attended discrete measurement.

States no expected or acceptable specific conductance value for any water type. There is no freshwater, brackish, estuarine, or drinking-water window and no action level at which a reading should be rejected as implausible. The only concentration figures a reader gets are calibration standard values (100, 500, 1,413, 12,900 microsiemens per centimeter) and the 5 to 1,100 microsiemens per centimeter range of the SRS uncertainty study.

Reproduces no low-pH temperature-compensation method. For samples with pH below 4 the chapter states the standard factors can be 50 percent in error and defers entirely to McCleskey (2013); the alternative algorithm itself appears nowhere, so the corpus carries the requirement without the method.

Gives no rule for choosing a temperature-compensation factor within the 0.019 to 0.020 per degree Celsius range, and no table of the factor by dominant ion or water type, even though section 1.1 states that conductivity changes 0.5 to 3 percent per degree Celsius depending on the ionic species present.

Gives no salinity or total-dissolved-solids conversion beyond the ratio of TDS in milligrams per liter to specific conductance in microsiemens per centimeter being 0.5 to 0.9. The practical salinity scale is cited (Lewis, 1980) but no equation, coefficient, or table for computing salinity from specific conductance appears.

Gives no numeric suspended-sediment or turbidity threshold at which a sample must be filtered before measurement. Filtering is triggered only by qualitative language ('a lot of suspended sediment', 'interfere with the stability of the readings'), and the only numeric test is applied after the fact, by comparing the filtered and unfiltered results.

Gives no storage requirement, shelf life, or opened-bottle expiry for potassium chloride calibration standards beyond 'do not use expired standards', and no instruction on how standards should be transported or stored in the field.

Gives no instrument specification a buyer could procure against. There is no required resolution in microsiemens per centimeter, no method detection limit, and no stated lower measurable limit other than the expectation that deionized water reads below 3 microsiemens per centimeter; the only instrument accuracy figure in the chapter is the plus or minus 5 percent accuracy of the built-in temperature compensation.

Gives no guidance for water colder than 5 degrees Celsius. Table 6.3-2 tabulates KCl standard conductivities from 0 to 50 degrees Celsius, but every procedural temperature window in the chapter is 5 to 35 degrees Celsius, with an explicit caution above 35 degrees Celsius and silence below 5 degrees Celsius; nothing is said about measuring under ice or in near-freezing water.

Describes no interference between the conductivity sensor and the other sensors on a multiparameter sonde apart from two ordering rules (calibrate specific conductance before pH; place the specific conductance probe upstream of the pH electrode in a flow cell). Nothing is said about interaction with dissolved-oxygen, ORP, or turbidity sensors sharing the same sonde.
summary.notes:
Chunk coverage: all 44 chunks are recorded. Chunks 7, 10, and 16 (pre-existing) and chunks 19, 22, 25, 28, 31, 34, 37, and 40 are pure 400-character overlap from the preceding chunk plus a page marker, with no original text; they carry empty claim arrays. Chunk 19 in particular repeats the whole tail of chunk 18 (the section 3.3 preamble and calibration step 1), which is attributed to chunk 18.
Newly recovered chunks 1 and 2 are front matter: the suggested citation and ISSN, the Contents dot leaders, and the lists of figures and tables. Chunks 42 and 43 are References Cited plus the back cover. All four correctly yield no claims.
Figure 6.3-1 is damaged in the corpus. Its caption survives in chunks 13 and 14 ('Diagram showing general guidelines for selecting an electrical conductivity probe with the optimum cell constant', modified from the YSI Model 3200 Operations Manual), but the diagram body -- the part that actually maps a cell constant to a conductance range -- appears nowhere as text. Two claims in the document point at this figure; neither can be resolved from the corpus.
Equation 3 arrives OCR-scrambled in chunk 41. It extracts as 'TD \t mg/L / specific conductance in \u03bcS/cm / S in  0.5 to 0.9 \t (3)', with the letters of 'TDS in' split around the fraction. The 0.5 to 0.9 ratio is recoverable only from the sentence preceding it, which is what the claim quotes.
Table 6.3-3 (chunk 38) arrives with its caption, its unit bracket, and both column headers ('Symptom', 'Possible cause and corrective action') intact, so it is not a headerless grid; but the symptom labels and the corrective-action bullets are interleaved on shared lines ('Erratic readings \t \u2022 Loose or defective connections'), and the chunk also runs straight into the tail of section 6.1 and the start of section 7.0, so it mixes the table with unrelated body text. Chunk 38 also uses the masculine ordinal character in 'about 25 \u00baC' where the rest of the document uses the degree sign; the quote preserves it verbatim.
The acceptance criterion 'plus or minus 5 microsiemens per centimeter for measurements at or below 100, or plus or minus 3 percent above 100' is restated at least ten times across sections 3.3, 4.1, 4.1.1, 4.1.2, 4.2.1, 4.2.2, 4.3.1, 6.1, and table 6.3-3. It serves six distinct roles: calibration check-standard tolerance, field stability criterion, replicate subsample agreement, filtered-versus-unfiltered divergence trigger, well-purge stability criterion (five readings 3 to 5 minutes apart), and the temperature-compensation diagnostic. Retrieval for it will have many legitimate supporting chunks, so any fixture built on it must name which of the six uses it means.
Cross-document value: this chapter carries the derivation that the operator-facing documents in this corpus lack. It states the reference temperature explicitly ('Specific conductance (and electrical conductivity) data are reported at 25 \u00b0C', chunk 35), gives the linear temperature-compensation factor as 0.019 to 0.020 per degree Celsius in four separate places (chunks 9, 14, 23, and 35), bounds its validity to pH 4 to 11 and 5 to 35 degrees Celsius, and states the 50 percent error it produces outside that pH window. 0.019 to 0.020 per degree Celsius is 1.9 to 2.0 percent per degree Celsius, so a bare '~2 percent per degree C' figure elsewhere in the corpus is consistent with this chapter but unqualified by the pH and temperature bounds that this chapter attaches to it.
This chapter is also the only place in the corpus that carries a specific conductance calibration procedure at all; the conductivity probe datasheet gives specifications without any method.
The total of 180 claims exceeds the 60-150 band in the brief because sections 3.3 and 4.0 through 4.3 are almost entirely numbered procedural steps, each carrying an independently checkable requirement, and because the 44 chunks include 11 that are pure overlap and contribute none.
